title: bug: an environment can never be retired, so the health sweep probes dead URLs forever
description:
MEASURED 2026-09-08 at HEAD 7622a2e8 by worker-bcaa6d5e from the epic-final row task-99f364e3, hunting the specific cross-band shape "a probe schedule that outlives the environment it probes".

THE SYMBOL. `apps/daemon/src/monitoring/health-probe-ring.ts:240 createHealthProbeJob` enumerates what to probe as
  [...readDeployLedger(options.store, options.projectId).keys()].filter(name => !skip.has(name))
`readDeployLedger` derives its environment set from DEPLOY RECEIPTS, which are append-only. An environment therefore enters the sweep on its first deploy and can never leave it.

AND THERE IS NO WAY OUT, which is the part that makes this real rather than theoretical: `git grep -l "deployment.destroy\|environment.destroy\|deployment.teardown\|ENVIRONMENT_DESTROY" -- apps packages` returns NOTHING. The platform has no retire, destroy or teardown command for an environment at any layer. So an operator who stands up a preview environment, uses it and tears the containers down by hand has no way to tell the daemon it is gone; the sweep keeps probing its URL on every tick, forever, and every one of those ticks records a DOWN sample in the ring and can open an incident.

WHAT IS ALREADY RIGHT, so a fix does not re-derive it: the per-environment job (`createEnvironmentHealthProbeJob`) reads an `active()` predicate PER TICK and probes nothing when the interval record has been cleared, and the sweep already honours a `dedicated` skip set read per tick. The mechanism for "stop probing this one" exists at the dedicated-job granularity; what is missing is any operator-reachable way to say an environment is retired, and the sweep's use of an append-only ledger as its roster.

NOT THE SAME AS THE DEDICATED-INTERVAL CASE ALREADY SHIPPED by task-078232fb: clearing an interval moves an environment from its dedicated job BACK to the sweep. It does not retire it.

DEFINITION OF DONE
1. An operator can retire an environment through a real command, and the health sweep stops enumerating it — proven by a probe tick that records nothing for the retired name.
2. Retirement is a durable, replayable fact, not in-memory state: a daemon restart does not resurrect the retired environment into the sweep.
3. The deploy ledger stays append-only. Retirement is a separate fact layered over it, never a receipt deletion.
4. Retiring an environment does not destroy its history: its probe ring and its receipts stay readable.
5. `pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test` EXIT 0 with its count line quoted.
definitionOfDone: An operator-reachable command retires an environment, and createHealthProbeJob stops enumerating it: a probe tick after retirement records no sample for that name.
Retirement is durable and replayable — a daemon restart does not resurrect the retired environment into the sweep.
The deploy ledger stays append-only: retirement is a fact layered over it, never a receipt deletion, and the retired environment's probe ring and receipts stay readable.
pnpm --filter @moe/daemon test EXIT 0 with its Test Files count line quoted.

implementationPlan.description:
THE NEGATIVE HALF: RETIREMENT IS NOT DESTRUCTION, AND IT IS NOT ESCAPABLE (parent DoD 3).

(a) HISTORY SURVIVES. After the retirement in step 2, assert the retired environment's deploy receipts are still readable through `readDeployLedger` AND that its existing probe-ring samples are still readable. The parent's DoD 3 says the ledger stays append-only and retirement is a fact layered over it — this is where that is proven end to end rather than per-module. Assert on the receipts' CONTENT, not merely that a call returned: a reader that silently returns an empty set would pass a shallow check.

(b) THE LEDGER WAS NOT MUTATED. The ledger derives its environment set from append-only receipts, so a "fix" that worked by removing a receipt would also make step 2 pass. Assert the receipt count and the environment set are unchanged by the retirement.

(c) A RETIRED ENVIRONMENT THAT OWNS A DEDICATED INTERVAL STILL STOPS. The sweep and the per-environment job are two paths (`createHealthProbeJob` and `createEnvironmentHealthProbeJob`), and an environment with its own interval is served by the second. Child 2 covers this in isolation; assert it here through the real command so retirement cannot be escaped by holding an interval.

(d) A DEPLOY AFTER RETIREMENT. Decide and pin the answer rather than leaving it undefined: if an operator retires an environment and then deploys to it again, does it come back into the sweep? Whatever the children implemented, this arm records it. An undefined answer here is a defect the next operator finds in production.
implementationPlan.note:
TWO MORE ARMS IN THE SAME FILE (now 349 lines, under the 400 cap; peers in this directory run 293-311). Still NO production code touched.

ARM 2 — (a) HISTORY SURVIVES + (b) LEDGER NOT MUTATED, asserted on CONTENT. Captures the ledger and the ring BEFORE the operator's command, then after it asserts: the environment SET is still exactly ["production","staging"] (a NAMED literal, so a ledger emptied on both sides cannot pass the deep-equality beside it); staging still holds exactly 1 receipt; and the receipt's current still carries outcome DEPLOYED, sha a*40 and url http://127.0.0.1:49211 — the three fields an operator reads to answer "what was there". Then the ring still holds the samples it held, with the pre-retirement read pinned to a literal so an empty-vs-empty comparison cannot pass.

ARM 3 — (c) NOT ESCAPABLE BY AN INTERVAL + (d) A DEPLOY ENDS IT, one window because it is one story. staging gets a 10s dedicated interval, is served by createEnvironmentHealthProbeJob (3 samples over 30s, cross-checked against the HTTP count), is retired THROUGH THE REAL COMMAND, and then stays at 3 across a window spanning several dedicated ticks AND a full default sweep tick — so a retirement honoured by only one of the two probe paths would show as growth. Production advances over the same window, so the daemon is demonstrably alive. It then survives a restart on the dedicated path too, which matters because restore resolution (composition :758) is a THIRD reader of the fact and a permissive fallback there would re-arm the job.

(d) THE ANSWER IS PINNED: A NEW SUCCESSFUL DEPLOY ENDS RETIREMENT. environment-retirement-record.ts:74 scopes a retirement to latestSuccessful(state) === cutoff, so a later DEPLOYED receipt supersedes the observed generation and probing resumes with no un-retire command and no restart. The arm also proves retirement is REPEATABLE, not one-shot: the operator retires again, a SECOND durable event lands (readEvents length 2), probing stops again, and the ledger grew by exactly the one receipt the deploy appended.

A REAL TIMING FACT THIS ARM FOUND, and the reason it first went red. After a restart a retired environment gets NO dedicated arm at all (composition :669 "Retired entries are not armed"). When a later deploy un-retires it, the arm comes back only when reconcileProbeSchedules runs — and that runs on the SWEEP's tick. So the wait after a redeploy is bounded by the DEFAULT 60s interval EVEN FOR AN ENVIRONMENT THAT OWNS A FASTER ONE. My first window advanced only 30s, the count stayed at 3, and it read exactly like "a redeploy does not un-retire" — the wrong conclusion, from a short window rather than a defect. The corrected window is DEFAULT_PROBE_INTERVAL_MS + 10_000 and the reason is written into the arm so the next reader does not re-derive it. Not a defect: child 2's own arm waits the same way.

DRILLS — 6 CELLS TOTAL, ALL PROCESS-LOCAL, NOTHING ON DISK MUTATED. Same out-of-tree config; every mutation asserts its own anchor and buildEnd throws on zero applications and prints the count.
- control (rerun with all 3 arms): Test Files 1 passed (1) / Tests 3 passed (3), applied=0.
- retirement-not-durable: RED, arm 1 only, at :225. applied=1.
- sweep-ignores-retirement: RED, arm 1 only, at :225. applied=1.
- dedicated-escapes-retirement (drops the retirement term from the per-environment job's active predicate at composition :662): RED, ARM 3 ONLY, at :316 — "expected 3, received 9", the dedicated job kept probing at 10s across a 60s window. Arms 1 and 2 stay GREEN because they use no interval. Clean isolation of the 3(c) claim.
- ledger-drops-receipts (readDeployLedger skips staging receipts — the REJECTED "just delete the receipts" design DoD 3 forbids): RED, ALL THREE arms. Arm 2 reds at :253 STAGING_ABSENT_FROM_LEDGER. Reddening all three is correct rather than blunt: destroying the receipts destroys the whole feature, which is why the design was rejected.
- receipt-content-corrupted (receipt still EXISTS and still probes; only its url is rewritten to 0.0.0.0): RED, ARM 2 ONLY, at :271 with the exact diff "http://127.0.0.1:49211" vs "http://0.0.0.0:49211". This is the cell that isolates step 3(a)'s "assert on CONTENT, not merely that a call returned" — the receipt is present and healthy and the arm still catches it.

FOCUSED RUN, foreground: cd apps/daemon && npx vitest run --root . --config package.json --maxWorkers=4 --testTimeout=30000 src/monitoring/environment-retirement-restart.test.ts -> EXIT 0, "Test Files 1 passed (1)", "Tests 3 passed (3)".

1. SHARED RECORD INSTANCE — the split's named characteristic failure. NOT PRESENT, and the plan's framing was wrong in a way worth recording. The registry (daemon-command-registry.ts:248) and the composition (:643) each construct their OWN EnvironmentRetirementRecord. That is fine, and instance identity is the wrong thing to look at: the record is a STATELESS FACADE whose replay() re-reads store.readEvents on every read/stored/write with no memoisation, so visibility comes from same-`store` + same-`projectId`. Both get exactly those from createDaemonCommandPorts at composition :297-298. The interval record already ships two instances over one store and is documented as correct. What actually proves the wiring is not a code reading but the retirement-not-durable drill: drop the store.commit and arm 1 reds at :225 with the retirement resurrecting after the restart.

2. ROSTER ARM DIRECTION — global rail 9. BOTH directions, correctly. daemon-store-dependencies.test.ts:1246 takes `served` from `deps.registry.keys()`, the DISPATCH SEAM, not from the roster constant, and asserts `expect(served).toEqual(advertised)` — one equality stating both directions — then names retire_environment and set_probe_interval on the served side so a wholesale two-sided deletion cannot pass. Nothing for this row to add.

3. REFUSALS AS STABLE CODES WITH THEIR LAYER. `grep 'throw new Error("'` over both retirement modules returns NOTHING: every refusal is a typed EnvironmentRetirementCode with layer DAEMON_INGRESS, and the edge forwards the record's refusal UNRESTAMPED. Child 3's arms assert code AND layer AND that the port was reached, so the record's layer cannot be a label the edge typed for itself. The operator fence answers at a DIFFERENT layer (OPERATOR_PRINCIPAL_REQUIRED@DAEMON_AUTHORIZATION) with a positive control proving the same payload is accepted through the operator principal.

4. EPIC RAIL 4 — DOES ANYTHING FAIL TO STOP. Three readers of the retirement fact, all per-call, all exercised: composition :662 (dedicated job's active predicate), :676 (schedule reconciliation), :758 (restore resolution — the one a permissive fallback would use to re-arm a retired job). Arm 3 crosses all three by retiring a dedicated-interval environment and then restarting. Every arm asserts in its `finally`, therefore on the FAILURE path too, that timer.arms.filter(arm => !arm.cleared) is empty. Zero leaked temp dirs measured after every run. No real socket is opened: the probe HTTP port is an injected callback.

(a) CONCURRENT RETIREMENT. The record commits at expectedVersion = the replayed version, so two operators retiring the same environment simultaneously give one ENVIRONMENT_RETIREMENT_STORE_FAILED. A retry then returns accept(true) because the environment is already retired, so it is self-healing, but the first caller sees a store-fault code for what is really a lost race. No arm covers it.

ARCHITECT architect-5385678f 2026-09-08 — SPLIT, NOT PLANNED AS ONE ROW. Four children filed in PLANNING, parent dependsOn set to all four, parent replanned as the integration proof (4 steps, 0 production files).

WHY THE SPLIT WAS FORCED, measured rather than judged. This row needs a new operator command kind. A full-tree census of the existing sibling kind — `git grep -l "monitoring.set_probe_interval" -- .` — returns **19 non-.moe files**: `packages/contracts/src/runtime/runtime-vocabulary.ts:102`, `packages/control-room-client/src/generated/generated-client.ts`, `apps/daemon/src/orchestrator/agent-spawn-contract.ts`, the command's own contracts module, and roster/allowlist arms in daemon-command-vocabulary.test.ts, mcp-tool-allowlist.test.ts, daemon-store-dependencies.test.ts, daemon-command-registry.test.ts, daemon-v2-command-registry.test.ts, daemon-command-registry-human-approver.test.ts, mcp-main.test.ts, runtime-contract.test.ts and agent-wrapper.test.ts. That is past `moe.submit_plan`'s 10-file hard reject **before** a single line of retirement logic. Any plan that fit the cap would have had to drop the kind, the mirrors or the arms — each omission ships a capability that does not work.

THE CHILDREN, cut on the layer boundary the code already has (SPIDR "Interface"):
- **140.1 task-a2dd124fed1b4b9889c626824fc0a6fb** — the durable retirement record (leaf). Mirrors `probe-interval-record.ts`. Durable, replayable, layered over the append-only ledger. Independent.
- **140.2 task-f18bddee94cf4b559272d23d53f6180e** — the sweep honours it. `health-probe-ring.ts` + composition wiring. dependsOn 140.1.
- **140.3 task-509f043721ac491baad33b0d6771a958** — publishes `monitoring.retire_environment` across the shared roster and all four digest mirrors, with the control-room leg epic rail 1 mandates. Independent, parallel with 140.1.
- **140.4 task-1714234a8b5341f3b652cc5279a1f75e** — the daemon command edge behind the operator fence, writing the 140.1 fact. dependsOn 140.1, 140.2, 140.3.

**ORDERING IS A SAFETY CONSTRAINT, not paperwork.** The READER (140.2) lands before the WRITER (140.4). If the command shipped first, an operator could retire an environment and the sweep would keep probing it — the product would advertise a capability that does not work, which is the worst of the three possible orders.
